title: China extends pause on rare-earth export curbs only to 10 January, keeping India exposed
dek: A two-month extension keeps the October 2025 controls, including a rule reaching foreign-made goods, on hold. The April 2025 licensing that disrupted Indian carmakers stays in force.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China has extended its suspension of a sweeping package of rare-earth, battery and superhard-material export controls by two months, to 10 January 2027, after the earlier pause ran out on 10 November. The short extension, tied to Beijing's trade truce with Washington, leaves India, which is not part of that deal, facing a fresh deadline in eight weeks.

The decision was published on Monday as Announcement No. 58 of 2026 of the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and the General Administration of Customs. "With approval, from 11 November 2026 to 10 January 2027," it said, six announcements issued in October 2025 "will continue to be suspended". The notice gave no reason and no other details.

## What stays on hold, and what does not

The suspended measures, announced on 9 October 2025, would require export licences for rare-earth mining, separation and magnet-making equipment and technology; for lithium batteries and their cathode and graphite anode materials; and for industrial synthetic-diamond products. They also include what is often called the extraterritorial rule, under which foreign-made goods containing Chinese-origin rare earths worth 0.1% or more of their value would need a Chinese licence, according to analyses of the original notices.

The extension does not touch China's licensing regime of 4 April 2025, which requires permits to export seven medium and heavy rare earths, including dysprosium and terbium, that go into the permanent magnets used in electric-vehicle motors and electronics. That regime remains fully in force. A separate pause on China's December 2024 ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the United States runs out on 27 November and was not mentioned in Monday's notice.

At the commerce ministry's weekly briefing on Thursday, spokesperson He Yadong spoke about a reciprocal tariff-cutting framework with the United States, which he said "helps stabilise and expand China-US bilateral trade", and said the two sides were in close communication, with progress to be "announced in due course". He did not address rare earths in the remarks reported from the briefing. When it announced the October 2025 package, the commerce ministry said the controls were meant to safeguard national security and interests.

## The risk for India

India depends on China for about 85% of its rare-earth magnets, according to a September 2026 report by the Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA) and Boston Consulting Group, which put China's share of global rare-earth processing at about 90%. The report described the November deadline as a "risk of access rather than of price"; that risk has now moved to 10 January.

Indian manufacturers have already felt the April 2025 controls. China's magnet exports fell by about three-quarters year on year in May 2025, and several Indian vehicle makers warned that they had only weeks of stock. The MEA said in October 2025 that some Indian companies had received Chinese licences to import magnets. In November 2025, the Union Cabinet approved a scheme of about Rs 7,300 crore to build domestic capacity for sintered rare-earth permanent magnets of about 6,000 tonnes a year, which will take years to come on stream.

The extraterritorial rule is the part that matters most for India's export ambitions. If it is ever applied, Indian makers of electronics, motors and components that use Chinese rare earths could need Beijing's permission to sell their products abroad, including to the United States. Because the suspension is renewed in short steps tied to US-China talks, its continuation depends on a negotiation in which India has no seat.

## What happens next

- 18-19 November: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders meet in Shenzhen, where a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump is expected.
- 27 November: China's suspension of its gallium, germanium and antimony ban for the United States is due to lapse.
- 10 January 2027: the extended suspension of the October 2025 package ends unless it is renewed again.
